title: Ezekiel 36:33–38
context: The Lord GOD continues: on the day he cleanses Israel from its iniquities, the cities will be inhabited, the ruins rebuilt, and the desolate land tilled (36:33–34). Passers-by will say the land has become “like the garden of Eden” (36:35; compare Genesis 2:8 and Isaiah 51:3). The surrounding nations will know that the LORD has rebuilt and replanted, for he has spoken and will do it (36:36). The LORD also says he will let the house of Israel inquire of him for this, and he will multiply them like the flocks brought to Jerusalem at the appointed feasts (36:37–38). On how prayer relates to God’s promised purpose (36:37), see the Joshua 10:14 box. Both traditions read the unit as a picture of restoration that makes the LORD known.

verses.text: “ ‘The Lord GOD says: “In the day that I cleanse you from all your iniquities, I will cause the cities to be inhabited and the waste places will be built.
verses.arminianNotes: On the day the LORD cleanses them from iniquity, the cities will be inhabited and the ruins rebuilt. Arminian readers see inner cleansing and outward restoration belonging together in God’s plan.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the cleansing as the foundation of the land’s renewal. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as linking forgiveness and rebuilding, so that restored people and restored land go together.

verses.text: The land that was desolate will be tilled instead of being a desolation in the sight of all who passed by.
verses.arminianNotes: The desolate land will be tilled instead of lying waste before passers-by. Arminian readers see the reversal of shame, as a land once observed in ruin is seen flourishing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s renewing work made visible to all. Both traditions read the verse as a simple but powerful picture of restoration, with fields worked again.

verses.text: They will say, ‘This land that was desolate has become like the garden of Eden. The waste, desolate, and ruined cities are fortified and inhabited.’
verses.arminianNotes: People will say the desolate land has become like the garden of Eden, with cities fortified and inhabited. Arminian readers see the image of Eden, compare Genesis 2:8 by reference, as abundant restored blessing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the parallel image in Isaiah 51:3 by reference, where the LORD makes Zion’s wilderness like Eden. Shared ground: both traditions read like Eden as a comparison of beauty and fruitfulness, without pressing it further.

verses.text: Then the nations that are left around you will know that I, the LORD, have built the ruined places and planted that which was desolate. I, the LORD, have spoken it, and I will do it.”
verses.arminianNotes: The surrounding nations will know that the LORD has rebuilt and replanted; he has spoken and will do it. Arminian readers see God’s restoring work as a witness to the nations, inviting them to know him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the formula I have spoken it, and I will do it as underscoring God’s faithfulness. Both traditions read the verse as confidence that the LORD’s promises are as sure as his judgments proved to be.

verses.text: “ ‘The Lord GOD says: “For this, moreover, I will be inquired of by the house of Israel, to do it for them: I will increase them with men like a flock.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will let the house of Israel inquire of him for this, and he will increase them like a flock. Arminian readers see prayer as a real part of how God brings about restoration with his people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see prayer as the means God ordains for fulfilling what he has promised. Shared ground: both traditions agree that God invites his people to ask; on how prayer relates to his purpose, see the Joshua 10:14 box.

verses.text: As the flock for sacrifice, as the flock of Jerusalem in her appointed feasts, so the waste cities will be filled with flocks of men. Then they will know that I am the LORD.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The waste cities will be filled with people like the flocks of Jerusalem at the appointed feasts. Arminian readers see a picture of joyful abundance, crowds gathered as at festival times.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the image of sacrificial flocks pointing to restored worship as well as restored population. Both traditions read the closing refrain, they will know that I am the LORD, as the goal of the whole chapter.
